title: Concurrency in LLD: thread-safety, locks, producer-consumer, thread-safe singleton
relevance: High — LLD / machine-coding follow-ups and senior LLD rounds (parking lot double-book, logging, inventory, bounded queue, connection pool); Flipkart/Uber/Swiggy machine coding + FAANG/experienced “make it thread-safe”
company_notes: Campus / machine coding (India product cos): often optional until the happy path works — then “make parking / booking / logging thread-safe”; Flipkart, Uber, Swiggy, Amazon loops commonly add this as a follow-up. Experienced / SDE-2+ LLD: concurrency is in-scope from the start (rate limiter, connection pool, scheduler, bounded queue, concurrent cache); Hello Interview–style correctness/coordination/scarcity language scores well. Frequency: nearly every shared-mutable LLD design gets a concurrency probe at mid-level; explicit “design a blocking queue / thread pool” prompts are common at product cos and FAANG-adjacent loops once OOP/patterns are assumed.

phases.goal: Establish what thread-safety means and how to diagnose Correctness vs Coordination vs Scarcity before picking a primitive.

must_hit.point: Thread-safety means correct results under concurrent access: no lost updates, no torn reads, and visibility of writes across threads (happens-before)—not merely “I used a lock somewhere.”
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names visibility/happens-before alongside mutual exclusion, not only locking.

must_hit.point: A race/critical section is shared mutable state with overlapping read-modify-write or check-then-act (two threads both see “spot free” / “qty=1” and both commit); fix by making check+act atomic under one lock or one atomic op.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a check-then-act example and says the check and act must be one atomic critical section.

must_hit.point: Hello Interview interview map: diagnose Correctness (locks/atomics) → Coordination (blocking queue / producer-consumer) → Scarcity (semaphore / pool); do not reach for a thread pool before the shared-state race is fixed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders the three categories and refuses thread-pool-first when the bug is a shared-state race.

probes: What does thread-safety require beyond “using a lock,” and how do you classify a concurrency bug as Correctness, Coordination, or Scarcity?

hints.1: Separate mutual exclusion from whether other threads can even see your writes.
hints.2: Ask whether the failure is a shared-state race, a handoff/wait problem, or a limited resource.
hints.3: Thread-safety = no lost updates/torn reads + happens-before visibility; map Correctness→locks/atomics, Coordination→blocking queue/P-C, Scarcity→semaphore/pool—fix the race before adding a pool.

phases.goal: Show how locks, condition waiting, BlockingQueue producer-consumer, atomics, deadlock prevention, and thread-safe Singleton are implemented in interview answers.

must_hit.point: Locks (mutex / synchronized / ReentrantLock) give mutual exclusion for multi-field invariants; prefer the smallest critical section that still keeps the invariant; coarse lock is simpler with less parallelism, fine-grained gives more throughput with deadlock risk.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States smallest-safe critical section and contrasts coarse simplicity vs fine-grained throughput/deadlock.

must_hit.point: Condition waiting with wait/notify or Condition.await/signal must always wait in a while (not if) re-checking the predicate because of spurious wakeups and lost notify; for producer-consumer prefer BlockingQueue put/take over hand-rolled wait/notify—multi-producer/multi-consumer safe, shut down with poison pills or interrupt + shutdownNow.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Insists on while-recheck and names BlockingQueue put/take as the interview default for P-C.

must_hit.point: Bounded producer-consumer: producers put into a buffer, consumers take; a bounded queue gives backpressure (producer blocks when full) and prevents unbounded memory growth; empty → consumer blocks efficiently (no busy-spin). Atomics/CAS suit single counters/flags but are not enough when two fields must change together (need a lock or redesign). Deadlock is circular wait—prevent with consistent lock order, tryLock+backoff, or fewer locks; know starvation/livelock as progress cousins.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links bounded buffer to backpressure, limits CAS to single-variable RMW, and names ordered locks/tryLock for deadlock.

must_hit.point: Thread-safe Singleton Java checklist: naive lazy is broken → synchronized getInstance → DCL + volatile → Bill Pugh static holder → enum Singleton (serialization/reflection-safe); eager init is fine if always needed; prefer DI/shared instance unless truly process-global.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Sketches the progression and names volatile on DCL plus holder or enum as strong answers.

probes: Walk through locking a multi-field invariant, waiting on a condition correctly, implementing bounded producer-consumer with BlockingQueue, and making a Java Singleton thread-safe.

hints.1: Start from what is shared and what must stay consistent, then pick lock vs queue vs atomic.
hints.2: Smallest critical section; while around wait; BlockingQueue for P-C; DCL needs volatile; enum/holder beat naive lazy.
hints.3: Mutex/synchronized/ReentrantLock for multi-field invariants; while-recheck wait/notify; bounded buffer backpressure via put/take; CAS only for single counters; Singleton: synchronized → DCL+volatile → Bill Pugh → enum.

phases.goal: Choose coarse vs fine locks, volatile vs compound synchronization, BlockingQueue vs hand-rolled waiting, ConcurrentHashMap vs external locks, and Singleton vs DI.

must_hit.point: Coarse-grained locking is simpler and safer but reduces parallelism; fine-grained locking raises throughput and deadlock risk—interviewers want the shared resource locked (spot map, inventory row), not every unrelated method synchronized on the whole class.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects class-wide sync by default and ties lock grain to the shared resource and deadlock risk.

must_hit.point: volatile gives visibility for a single field, not atomic check-then-act on compound state; DCL needs volatile so a half-constructed Singleton is not published. ConcurrentHashMap is great for independent key ops but multi-key invariants (transfer between two keys, check-then-put-if-absent across structures) still need external coordination.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates visibility from atomic compound updates and limits ConcurrentHashMap to independent-key cases.

must_hit.point: Prefer BlockingQueue over hand-rolled wait/notify for producer-consumer; leave synchronized for ReentrantLock when you need tryLock / interruptible acquire and unlock in try-finally. Unbounded queues coordinate without backpressure and can blow memory under burst—prefer capacity plus block/reject. Singleton instance creation being thread-safe does not make mutating methods thread-safe.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defaults to BlockingQueue, names tryLock as a ReentrantLock reason, and separates Singleton creation safety from method sync.

probes: When do you choose coarse vs fine locks, volatile vs a lock, BlockingQueue vs wait/notify, ConcurrentHashMap alone vs external locking, and Singleton vs DI?

hints.1: Ask what must be atomic together and whether the problem is visibility, handoff, or multi-key consistency.
hints.2: Lock the shared resource not the whole class; volatile ≠ compound check-then-act; BlockingQueue beats hand-rolled P-C; CHM does not cover multi-key invariants.
hints.3: Coarse = simple/less parallel; fine = throughput + deadlock risk; volatile for single-field visibility/DCL; BlockingQueue + bounded capacity for backpressure; CHM for independent keys only; Singleton creation ≠ method safety—prefer DI unless process-global.

phases.goal: Apply the Correctness/Coordination/Scarcity map and standard drills: park check-then-act, bounded queue, Singleton whiteboard, logging/cache, and account-transfer deadlock.

must_hit.point: Name-the-failure drill: (a) two parkers grab one spot → Correctness (lock/CAS); (b) API threads hand jobs to workers → Coordination (blocking queue / P-C); (c) at most 5 DB connections → Scarcity (semaphore / pool).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Labels each scenario with the Hello Interview category and a matching primitive.

must_hit.point: Check-then-act fix: park(vehicle) does findSpot + occupy under one lock (or CAS on spot state); synchronizing only findSpot still races. Bounded P-C drill: fixed-capacity buffer with ReentrantLock + two Conditions (notFull/notEmpty), then rewrite with ArrayBlockingQueue; state what changes for N producers / M consumers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Keeps find+occupy atomic and can sketch lock+two Conditions then ArrayBlockingQueue.

must_hit.point: Whiteboard Singleton: broken lazy → synchronized → DCL+volatile → Bill Pugh → enum; state one testing downside and the DI alternative. Logging/cache: locate the lock; ConcurrentHashMap may help; keep record write vs map put atomic when required. Deadlock hunt: transfer(A→B) locking both accounts reverse-order deadlocks; fix with ordered lock IDs or tryLock timeout.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Runs Singleton progression, names a logging/cache atomicity boundary, and fixes transfer deadlock with lock ordering or tryLock.

probes: Classify parking double-book, worker handoff, and a 5-connection pool; then fix park check-then-act, sketch a bounded queue, and hunt a reverse-order account-transfer deadlock.

hints.1: Tag each prompt as shared-state race, work handoff, or limited permits before coding.
hints.2: One lock around find+occupy; ReentrantLock + notFull/notEmpty or ArrayBlockingQueue; ordered locks on transfer.
hints.3: Spot race→Correctness; API→workers→Coordination; 5 DB connections→Scarcity; park under one lock; bounded buffer then BlockingQueue; Singleton DCL+volatile/holder/enum; transfer with ordered lock IDs or tryLock timeout.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Coarse lock is simpler with less parallelism; fine-grained raises throughput and deadlock risk. Prefer the smallest critical section that still keeps the invariant; lock the shared resource (spot map, inventory row), not every unrelated method on the whole class.
Stay with synchronized for straightforward mutual exclusion. Move to ReentrantLock when you need tryLock, interruptible acquire, multiple Conditions, and explicit unlock in try-finally.

tradeoffs.topic: volatile vs lock/atomic for compound state
tradeoffs.strong_answer: volatile gives visibility for a single field, not atomic check-then-act on compound state. DCL needs volatile so you do not publish a half-constructed Singleton. Multi-field invariants need a lock (or redesign); CAS/atomics suit single counters/flags only.

Hand-rolled wait/notify or Condition.await/signal must use while-recheck. Interview default for producer-consumer is BlockingQueue put/take (multi-producer/multi-consumer safe); shut down with poison pills or interrupt + shutdownNow.

Bounded queue gives backpressure—producer blocks when full—and prevents unbounded memory growth; empty consumers block without busy-spin. Unbounded coordination without backpressure risks memory blow-up under burst; prefer capacity plus block/reject.
ConcurrentHashMap is great for independent key ops. Multi-key invariants (transfer between two keys, check-then-put-if-absent across structures) still need external coordination.

Java progression: naive lazy (broken) → synchronized getInstance → DCL+volatile → Bill Pugh holder → enum (serialization/reflection-safe); eager init if always needed. Prefer DI/shared instance unless truly process-global; creation safety does not make mutating methods thread-safe.
Diagnose first: Correctness → locks/atomics; Coordination → blocking queue / producer-consumer; Scarcity → semaphore / pool. Do not reach for a thread pool before the shared-state race is fixed.

gotchas.trap: Assuming volatile is enough for compound check-then-act
gotchas.correction: volatile gives visibility for a single field, not atomic check-then-act on compound state. DCL needs volatile so you don’t publish a half-constructed Singleton.

gotchas.trap: Using if instead of while around wait
gotchas.correction: Spurious wakeups and multiple waiters mean you must always re-test the condition after waking—wait in a while, not if.

gotchas.trap: Synchronizing the whole class by default
gotchas.correction: Works but kills concurrency; lock the shared resource (spot map, inventory row), not every unrelated method.

gotchas.trap: Treating an unbounded queue as fine for coordination
gotchas.correction: Without backpressure, bursts can blow memory; prefer capacity plus block/reject.

gotchas.trap: Assuming Singleton is automatically thread-safe end-to-end
gotchas.correction: Only the instance creation story is covered; methods that mutate shared fields still need their own synchronization.
Great for independent key ops; multi-key invariants (transfer between two keys, check-then-put-if-absent across structures) still need external coordination.
